Tomato - Healthy.summary: The tomato foliage displays vibrant green coloration with no visible signs of chlorosis, necrosis, or fungal lesions.
Tomato - Healthy.symptoms: Normal leaf morphology, uniform chlorophyll distribution, intact leaf margins.
care_tips: Maintain consistent watering at the base of the plant to prevent soil splash onto lower leaves.
Ensure 6–8 hours of full direct sunlight daily.
Prune bottom suckers and foliage touching the ground to promote airflow.
Feed with a balanced potassium- and phosphorus-rich organic fertilizer.

Tomato - Early Blight.summary: A common fungal disease caused by Alternaria solani, often starting on older foliage near the ground.
Tomato - Early Blight.symptoms: Characteristic concentric rings ('target-board' or 'bullseye' pattern) with chlorotic yellow halos surrounding dark brown necrotic lesions.
care_tips: Immediately strip off and safely dispose of infected lower leaves; do not compost infected tissue.
Mulch soil around plants to prevent fungal spores in the soil from splashing onto leaves during watering.
Apply copper-based organic fungicide or bio-fungicide (Bacillus subtilis) at first symptom onset.
Water early in the morning and avoid overhead irrigation to keep the canopy dry.

Tomato - Late Blight.summary: A devastating water mold (oomycete) pathogen that can destroy foliage and fruit rapidly in cool, humid conditions.
Tomato - Late Blight.symptoms: Irregular dark, water-soaked lesions that turn purplish-brown; delicate white fuzzy fungal growth may appear on the leaf undersides in high humidity.
care_tips: Urgent action required: rogue and destroy severely affected plants immediately to protect neighboring crops.
Avoid overhead sprinkler watering; improve spacing for rapid drying.
Apply protective preventive copper fungicides when cool (60–70°F), wet weather is forecast.
Rotate nightshade crops with non-susceptible crops for at least 2–3 seasons.

Tomato - Leaf Mold.summary: A fungal pathogen common in high-humidity greenhouses and sheltered gardens with stagnant air.
Tomato - Leaf Mold.symptoms: Pale greenish-yellow chlorotic spots on upper leaf surfaces; olive-green to grayish velvety fungal cushions on corresponding undersides.
care_tips: Significantly boost ventilation and lower relative humidity below 85% in greenhouses.
Space plants generously and prune crowded interior leaf canopy.
Water only the root zone using drip lines.
Spray preventative bio-fungicide or copper soap on foliage under high humidity.

Potato - Healthy.summary: The potato vine shows strong vegetative health with uniform green compound leaves free of blight lesions.
Potato - Healthy.symptoms: Firm stems, vigorous leaflet growth, absence of spotting or premature defoliation.
care_tips: Hill soil up around stems as vines grow to protect developing tubers from sun exposure (greening).
Provide steady, even moisture, especially during tuber initiation and flowering.
Keep garden beds weed-free to eliminate wild alternate disease hosts.
Monitor underside of leaves weekly for early signs of beetle eggs or fungal spores.

Potato - Early Blight.summary: Fungal leaf spot disease that stresses potato vines and leads to premature foliage death if unchecked.
Potato - Early Blight.symptoms: Small brown angular spots enlarging into distinct concentric rings, frequently bordered by a yellow margin on mature leaves.
care_tips: Prune and discard infected leaflets from the lower tiers.
Maintain robust soil fertility, as nutrient-deficient plants are significantly more vulnerable to Alternaria.
Avoid handling potato foliage when wet from rain or dew.
Apply organic copper fungicide every 7–10 days during warm, humid conditions.

Potato - Late Blight.summary: The infamous historical pathogen responsible for the Irish Potato Famine; spreads explosively in damp conditions.
Potato - Late Blight.symptoms: Rapidly expanding water-soaked spots turning black or dark brown, often with a pale green halo; white fungal down on lower leaf surfaces.
care_tips: Remove and bag infected vines immediately; never allow blight spores to wash down into potato tubers.
Hill soil deeply over tubers to form a physical barrier against spores washing down from leaves.
Harvest tubers only in dry weather at least two weeks after vines have died or been cut.
Plant certified disease-free seed potatoes.

Apple - Healthy.summary: Apple leaves exhibit deep green coloration, clear serrated edges, and no fungal scabs or lesions.
Apple - Healthy.symptoms: Clean foliage, uniform texture, normal photosynthetic vigor.
care_tips: Perform annual dormant winter pruning to encourage sunlight penetration throughout the canopy.
Rake and compost or destroy fallen autumn leaves to eliminate overwintering spores.
Apply dormant horticultural oil in late winter before buds break.
Ensure proper root drainage and steady watering during fruit sizing.

Apple - Apple Scab.summary: The most prevalent apple fungal disease worldwide, impacting leaves and blemishing fruit skins.
Apple - Apple Scab.symptoms: Olive-green, velvety or velvety-brown spots with feathery, indistinct margins, later turning corky and dark brown.
care_tips: Meticulously rake and dispose of fallen leaves in autumn where the fungus overwinters.
Prune the tree canopy in winter to maximize rapid wind drying of morning dew.
Apply sulfur- or copper-based sprays in spring starting at green-tip bud stage.
Choose scab-resistant apple cultivars (e.g., Liberty, Freedom, Enterprise) for future plantings.

Apple - Black Rot.condition: Black Rot / Frogeye Leaf Spot (Botryosphaeria obtusa)
Apple - Black Rot.summary: A fungal pathogen affecting apple leaves (frogeye leaf spot phase), twigs (cankers), and maturing fruit.
Apple - Black Rot.symptoms: Small purple specks on leaves that enlarge into circular lesions with light brown centers and distinct dark purple margins ('frogeye' appearance).
care_tips: Prune out dead wood, fire-blight strikes, and mummified fruit, which are prime reservoirs for the fungus.
Sterilize pruning shears between cuts with 70% rubbing alcohol.
Apply captan- or copper-based fungicides from pink bud stage through petal fall.
Maintain tree vigor through balanced soil nutrition and summer irrigation.
